b: We’re officially into giving season, and with that–and the quiet holiday week upon us–it felt important to share what your support of independent media like ours has done this year. As noted in the linked piece, we’ve been in the same situation as so many other independent creators. Thanks to changes in how search functions work (err, don’t work), how algorithms do and do not prioritize content based on the whims of social media owners and shareholders, and the shrinking landscape of advertising, Book Riot has had to get creative in continuing to financial subsist.

One way has been through developing our All Access membership program. All Access members pay a monthly or annual fee to gain access to our New Release Index, paywalled newsletters and content, and ready access to our full archive of content, among a host of other perks. Across Book Riot, we keep everything that is not exclusive content for All Access members available for free for 30 days before putting it behind the gates.
What you may not know is this: it is thanks to All Access members that nothing published in Literary Activism ever goes behind a paywall.

For years, I’ve written about how important it is that democracy not die behind paywalls. One of many reasons that book banning and attacks on libraries and public education has been successful over the last few years is the death of local news covering these stories and too often, when these sorts of stories are covered, they’re paywalled. This means unless you have a subscription to that outlet or your public library has a database where you can access that newspaper, you don’t know what’s happening in your own community.

To paywall news, features, and the weekly roundup of book censorship news here would be a significant loss to readers globally who learn and depend upon the information to do good in their own communities.
All Access members are the reason this space remains freely available. Those monthly and annual subscribers support the work being done here and support the free access anyone has to it.

To thank All Access members–and, of course, to encourage those who may not know about the program or who have been on the fence about it to make the leap–here’s a look at five types of important Literary Activism stories that All Access members helped make possible this year. Whether you missed them the first time or want to revisit them, these pieces are a reminder of what’s possible when independent media is supported.
Ongoing Coverage of State-Level Book Bans and Breaking Book Censorship News

Utah has banned 26 books from every public and public charter school in the state this year alone. The total number of state-sanctioned book bans is now 45. That’s 45 books that have to be removed from every public school, even if the book was never once challenged in that school. The state’s mechanism is that three districts need to have removed the book; this means that a small number of districts in the state are driving bans for the whole state. It’s not happening without pushback, either–several authors filed a lawsuit against the state in January.

This year’s literary activism has also reported on breaking news as it happens. Among this year’s stories were Florida’s Commissioner of Education demanding all public and charter schools in the state proactively ban books–or face punishment, as well as a similar threat targeting public schools in Texas by the state’s (now booted!) Lieutenant Governor.

Literary Activism highlighted the federal-level book ban bills as they happened (and in many cases, before it was covered elsewhere), as well as the ongoing efforts by the Trump-Vance administration to destroy the only federal agency dedicated to public libraries, the Institute for Museum and Library Studies (IMLS). This year saw two legal victories for the IMLS, covered here and here, as well as ongoing efforts by the administration to enshittify the agency. Also covered? Efforts to revoke the federal e-Rate program that helps libraries pay for the internet access they provide communities.

The bill that would lead to public librarians being arrested for doing their jobs in Arkansas was not only covered, the greater context of the bill and its history was included, showcasing where and how bills like this have inspired copycat takes elsewhere. Arkansans dedicated to ending prison censorship also shared the wide-ranging impact of a new policy that would ban books to those on the inside; this story has a positive ending, as the new policy was not enacted in the state.
We also celebrated the passage of another Freedom to Read Law, this time in Massachusetts.
The Impact of Book Bans on Young People

There’s a generational impact of book bans on today’s teenagers. It’s not a question that teenagers in schools with full access to robust libraries are in a far better position than their peers in schools with no access to libraries, with limited access to libraries, or with censored collections.

It’s not just school libraries, either. Public libraries in several states have taken direction from partisan demands and have decimated teen collections and teen services. This has been especially rampant in South Carolina, where “young adult” literature has been reframed as being books for adults, thus, they need to be removed from teen areas.

As public schools and public libraries remove or restrict books, it’s not just the teens in those communities who are affected. So, too, are any future young readers hoping to get their hands on diverse, inclusive, and realistically-reflective literature in the future, as children’s publishing slows down production of such titles.

Months before Dolly Parton’s death lead to a rise in outlets covering her phenomenal youth literacy work through Imagination Library, Literary Activism highlighted where and how the program had been under attack across the country. Since that reporting, several more Imagination Library programs have found themselves at a breaking point, despite that increased positive attention for a couple of weeks this fall.
Primers and Guides to Literacy (and Illiteracy)

We’re in an era of information degradation, and one of the many reasons book banners have been able to achieve what they have since 2021 is their ability to wield misinformation and disinformation to their advantage. It’s hard even for outlets whose work is verifying information to keep on top of the flood of stories, and sometimes, something sounds true enough that diving deeper doesn’t seem necessary. That is, unfortunately, one of the tools of the trade and why it is so important to know how to check your sources. Yes, it’s an annoying and frustrating exercise, but it is important for accuracy and to help curtail the ways bad information is used to trick otherwise intelligent people.

Mis- and dis- information, ferried through the cherry-picking and decontextualization of passages, is precisely how book banners have developed their suite of tools that encourage people to challenge books in public institutions. Knowing about the tools book banners are using to target books helps literary advocates stay abreast of tactics being deployed and titles being challenged.

And speaking of manipulating information, a popular turn of phrase among book banners over the last year? “If it’s banned in prisons, why is it available in public schools?” The argument shows the entire hand of those banning literature, including how they do not care about the number one violation of First Amendment rights in the country: prison censorship. Here’s why that phrasing is so dangerous and disingenuous.
Book and Library Censorship Through History

Book censorship and literary discrimination is nothing new. It’s just been a couple of decades since it was happening with as much fervor as it has in the 2020s. With the death of Reverend Jesse Jackson in February, it felt like high time to talk about his role in The Greenville Eight–and where and how public libraries discriminated against marginalized communities through American history.

More recently, we’ve moved into our sixth year of coordinated book censorship and attacks on libraries. Although this data needs a slight update, thanks to this fall’s new PEN America report on the state of school book bans last year, this piece gives some numbers and insights into the who, what, where, when, and why of book ban data. We’ve also seen a new precedent being set when it comes to lawsuits being filed in this censorious era: librarians who are suing for wrongful termination over not removing diverse books or ending inclusive programs are winning via settlements. Here’s to hoping for a similar outcome in the Pickens County, South Carolina, lawsuit filed by the library’s former director.
Collaborations That Expand Knowledge and Community

My number one goal with Literary Activism every year, and especially this year, has been collaborative efforts to share information and advocacy opportunities. There are so many people doing tremendous literary advocacy and giving them the space to share their expertise is not only a chance to hear from an array of insightful, knowledgeable people but it is also showcasing what community and coalition building is all about.

This year’s collaborative efforts have included a deep dive into how legislators and the legal system have manipulated the law by dismantling the Miller Test and exploiting the “government speech” doctrine with Sarah Lamdan at the Office of Intellectual Freedom. Lamdan was also part of the team that also included Tasslyn Magnusson, Stephana Ferrell (Florida Freedom to Read Project), and Arielle Haughee (Freedom to Read Project) who put together a five year report about the advocacy efforts happening on the ground nationwide to protect the right to read from those doing the work. The same group worked with an array of books to prisoners advocacy groups to highlight what’s been happening with prison censorship over the last half decade (and how amazing just weeks after the report published, Wisconsin Books to Prisoners can once again send materials to those on the inside!).

We’ve also seen incredible guest pieces about prison censorship via Aaron Blumberg (see here, here, and here); about youth privacy and library card access from Amy Mikel (see here, here, and here); about a new digital tool to help librarians apply their intellectual freedom knowledge and skills from Library Futures; and what the decision in last year’s Little v. Llano County case means for book censorship in libraries nationwide from the lead plaintiff in the case herself, Leila Green Little.

Last but not least, ongoing support for Literary Activism has allowed young people–those most immediately impacted by book bans–to share their stories, too. Kylee Wood, a high school junior at Elizabethtown Area High School in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania and co-founder of the EAHS Student Activism Collective, talked about her experiences attending an institution where the school board has relentlessly targeted the books in classrooms and libraries. In her words, “I Cannot Let These Doctrines Be The Face of My Education.”

These stories and others like them are always free and will always remain free, and that is thanks to our All Access members. If you aren’t a member, consider signing up for an array of membership perks–as well as for helping support this crucial work that helps protect our democracy.
It is a quieter week for book censorship news due to the long holiday weekend in the United States.
Pikeland Consolidated School District 10 (IL) will not be removing The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian from curriculum.
Roaring Fork School District (CO) got a visit from the infamous book banning pastor who shows up across the country to school boards to make people mad about cherry-picked passages.

Somerset County School Board (MD) has been trying to pass one of the most extreme book banning measures in the country, and the state has told them they cannot because of their anti-book ban law. Now, the board showed an AI generated video about some of the books they don’t like to create shock. The obsession with the books is really not healthy nor normal.
The Alabama Public Library Service Board has now installed a new chair, who has been one of the biggest champions of pulling trans books out of public library youth sections statewide.
Wilson County Schools (TN) removed 400 books under the state’s book banning law Age Appropriate Materials Law and their plan for them is to simply throw them in the garbage.

This is a really good and thoughtful piece on where and how conservative Christians have taken over the Appomattox County library (VA). This includes changing the bylaws to allow them to be denied funding for not meeting state library laws so the library doesn’t have to include LGBTQ+ books.

Six months ago, I wrote about how funding for Dolly’s Imagination Library was being cut across the country in ways people were not paying attention to (and after Dolly’s death, several more places have cut this program, despite the donations that poured in). Here’s a note that Missouri’s program ends in December.

Arkansas’s Boone County Library has implemented new rules about library cards in the wake of Act 372. Now those with children’s cards can only access and borrow children’s books; those with teen cards can only access and borrow borrow books for teens or children; adult cards can access and borrow anything. Hope no student at all needs to do research with nonfiction books in the reference or adult sections of the library.
